standard.title: Complementary Events
standard.description: recognise that complementary events have a combined probability of one; use this relationship to calculate probabilities in applied contexts
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can assign probabilities to single-stage events and verify they sum to 1 (from AC9M7P01). Students understand the sample space.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students recognise complementary events, use P(A) + P(not A) = 1 to find probabilities, and apply this to practical contexts including AI applications.

nodes.label: Recognising complementary events
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students recognise complementary events as pairs that together cover all outcomes, and state that P(A) + P(not A) = 1.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify the complement of a given event and verify that P(A) + P(not A) = 1 for a specific example.
nodes.typical_width: Identify complementary pairs across varied contexts (dice, spinners, weather); state the relationship; distinguish complementary from mutually exclusive events.
wider: Investigate events that are not easily described by name — construct the complement explicitly from the sample space.
Explore whether two events can be both complementary and mutually exclusive — discuss what this tells you about the sample space.

response_modes.reason: Recognising complementary events requires reliable identification before the relationship can be applied strategically. Students who confuse complementary with mutually exclusive make systematic errors in node 2.

nodes.hinge_reason: Confusion between complementary and mutually exclusive events causes systematic errors in Node 2 — students who cannot reliably identify complements apply P(not A) = 1 − P(A) to the wrong events.
success_criteria: Correctly identifies the complement of a given event.
States P(A) + P(not A) = 1 and verifies it for a specific case.
Does not confuse complementary events with mutually exclusive events.

nodes.label: Using the complement relationship to calculate probabilities
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students use P(not A) = 1 − P(A) to calculate probabilities in applied contexts, including cases where finding the complement is more efficient than direct calculation.
nodes.minimum_width: Given P(A), find P(not A); apply to a practical problem where the complement is given and the event probability is required.
nodes.typical_width: Apply the complement relationship to a range of practical contexts; recognise when finding the complement is the more efficient strategy; apply to simple 'at least one' problems.
wider: Investigate how AI applications use complementary event probabilities when assessing binary outcomes — e.g. spam vs not spam, fraud vs not fraud.
Explore P(at least one) = 1 − P(none) for simple cases — apply to problems where direct calculation would require listing many outcomes.

response_modes.reason: The strategic insight — that finding the complement is sometimes easier — only develops across varied problem types. Students who only practise direct complement calculation miss the efficiency judgment that makes the relationship powerful.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: AI binary classification and the 'at least one' complement strategy offer advancing students rich applications — the connection to machine learning and the efficiency insight together make this a genuinely rich node for width investment.
success_criteria: Correctly calculates P(not A) given P(A) and vice versa.
Identifies at least one context where finding the complement is more efficient.
Applies the complement relationship correctly to a practical problem.
